extracted.intended_audience: improvisers, improv students, actors and comedy performers (especially those learning long-form/Harold)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluation criteria for performing and teaching long-form improvisation (the Harold) and general improv scene work — focused on truth, pattern-play, relationships, and practical scene mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pattern recognition & subversion (Harold)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use pattern recognition and subversion of audience expectations to create comedy without relying on explicit jokes; the Harold is a non-linear entertainment that 'remembers everything and wastes nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize repeated patterns and callbacks; build scenes so earlier details can be recognized and subverted later. The Harold involves six to seven players and many kinds of scenes (games, monologues, songs, skits) that feed patterns into one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: The truth is funny / honesty in the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The truth is funny' — honest discovery, observation, and reaction are better than contrived invention; be in the moment and truthful in performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground choices in honest impulses and reality of the scene; authenticity often yields the strongest, most satisfying laughs. Avoid contrivance for its own sake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Yes, & (agreement + addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Yes, & .' is the most important rule in improvisation — accept your partner's offer and add to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't just agree; agree and contribute new, scene-forward information. Use 'yes, and' to keep offers productive and to build the scene's reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your scene partner look good (generosity)
rubrics_metrics.description: A truly funny scene is the result of generosity — trying to make the other person (and his ideas) look as good as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize your partner's offers and take actions that support and elevate them. The best way to look good is to help others look good.

rubrics_metrics.name: No idea is a bad idea; make active choices
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't dismiss an idea out of hand; make active choices rather than passive ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active choices forward the scene; passive choices keep it stagnant. Embrace unexpected ideas as opportunities (the book's 'no idea is a bad idea' stance), but be mindful of whether an unusual choice actually serves the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen (not just hear) and respond to effects on partners
rubrics_metrics.description: Hearing and listening are different — truly listen to your partner and notice how your moves affect them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A player's move is not complete until they see how it affects their partner. Use listening to pick up patterns and to make choices that advance others and the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish relationships quickly
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on relationships between partners and establish them early (exercise: establish a scene in three lines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quickly creating relationship and context speeds scene progression and gives players material to play from. Strong relationships often produce clear emotional stakes and comedic dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and perceive a clear stage environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Create an environment on stage and perceive it internally — 'everything that we perceive is truly perceived inside the head.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent concrete physical/environmental details and behave as if they are real; the environment should affect characters' choices. The audience sees the environment through the actors' commitments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose specifics over generalities
rubrics_metrics.description: When making choices, specifics are always better than generalities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific details give scene partners and the audience concrete anchors to react to; specifics often generate richer connections and callbacks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide answers rather than ask questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking questions is less productive than providing answers for your partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give information and commitments that your partner can react to; avoid relying on questions to move the scene, which can stall momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer agreement over disagreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Disagreeing in a scene isn't very constructive; agreeing contributes to the scenario's growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disagreement sparingly and purposefully; generally accept offers and build on them to move the scene forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect scene ownership — don't steal scenes / avoid intrusive walk-ons
rubrics_metrics.description: Walk-ons (or other players) should not steal another player's scene or invade scenes that are progressing smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assist only when called for; don't jump in to hijack focus. Maintain ensemble awareness and scene economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use patterns and connections to generate laughs
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience laughter often comes from connections and pattern-completion; skilled players listen for patterns to exploit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop and reuse patterns so the audience can mentally complete connections; repetitions (often three times) and callbacks amplify payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disrupt routine to start action
rubrics_metrics.description: Action often begins when a routine is disrupted — the unexpected move can propel a scene into new territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce an interruption or twist to move from routine to dynamic play, but ensure it serves the emerging logic of the scene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid trying to be funny / don't rely on jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the biggest mistakes is attempting to be funny; jokes are often a last-ditch measure by insecure players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on truth, relationships, and strong scene choices rather than on inserting punchlines. Let humor emerge organically from the scene's reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal the art (make it look effortless)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Ars est celare artem' — the art is in concealing the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform so that the mechanics feel invisible; avoid telegraphing setup or stagecraft; let discoveries feel spontaneous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify and play the 'game' of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: The games or scenic structures are created on the spot; picking up the 'game move' separates strong game players from others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listen for recurring dynamics or a dominant comedic premise in the scene and lean into it; playing the game coherently produces bigger audience rewards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build character from the actor's truth
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'real character' in this approach consists of the actor himself plus an added point of view, preoccupation, or attitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the actor's center as a foundation and layer distinct attitudes or obsessions rather than inventing wholly foreign psychologies; be cautious of extremes and consider ethical/representational limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage pacing and scene length
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid letting a scene go on too long; watch for inappropriate focus or lack of specificity which can stall scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize when a scene has run its course and exit or shift; use scene economy to keep momentum and to make room for other beats in the Harold.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improv is a practiced skill — read + play
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning improv requires practice and group play; reading alone isn't sufficient to internalize the techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the book's exercises as prompts but rehearse and perform with others; return to foundational principles as you gain experience (read early, then re-read after practice).
